bills.title: Accelerating Access to Critical Therapies for ALS Reauthorization Act of 2026
bills.official_title: To amend the Accelerating Access to Critical Therapies for ALS Act to reauthorize the provisions of such Act through fiscal year 2031, and for other purposes.
bills.likelihoodReason: Introduced by Rep. Quigley (D-IL-5) with 103 cosponsors and cleared the House on July 22, 2026 before being placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders (Calendar No. 466). The measure extends an existing bipartisan program authored in 2021 without expanding federal spending authority beyond the existing $100M-per-year level, and adds oversight-tightening changes (adverse-event reporting, renewal-review safety and efficacy assessments) rather than new mandates that typically draw opposition. The main friction points are Senate calendar competition and any objections to the phase 2/3 combined-trial definition or the 5-year FDA action plan report burden — none large enough to defeat a rare-disease reauthorization with triple-digit House cosponsors.

referencedSources.label: Accelerating Access to Critical Therapies for ALS Act (Public Law 117-79)

bills.summary: This bill extends the 2021 Accelerating Access to Critical Therapies for ALS Act — which authorizes HHS and FDA grants for expanded-access research on investigational drugs for amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and other rare neurodegenerative diseases — through fiscal year 2031. It also tightens the underlying grants program by requiring safety and efficacy data on renewals, mandating prompt adverse-event reporting, expanding the "phase 3" definition to cover phase 2/3 combined trials, and requiring FDA to publish a new 5-year rare-neurodegenerative-disease action plan and follow-up report.
bills.brief: Extends the ALS investigational-drug grant program and its $100M-per-year authorization through fiscal year 2031, and adds safety-reporting and renewal-review requirements.

top_lines.headline: What the Underlying Program Does
subs: HHS awards grants to small-business drug sponsors running expanded-access programs for people with ALS not eligible for clinical trials
FDA-NIH Public-Private Partnership advances rare neurodegenerative disease research
Authorized at $100M per year since fiscal year 2022

top_lines.headline: What This Bill Extends
subs: Extends the $100M-per-year authorization of appropriations through fiscal year 2031
Extends the grants program sunset from September 30, 2026 to September 30, 2031

top_lines.headline: New Grant-Program Guardrails
subs: Grant renewals must include HHS review of enrollment, safety, and any available efficacy data
Grantees must promptly report new and serious adverse events and unexpected safety information
"Phase 3" now includes phase 2/3 combined trials that begin enrollment within a Secretary-set timeframe

top_lines.headline: FDA Action Plan Refresh
subs: FDA must publish a new 5-year rare-neurodegenerative-disease action plan within 18 months of enactment
FDA must publish a report on actions taken within 5 years of enactment

items.main: Extends the underlying Act's authorization of appropriations — $100M per year — through fiscal year 2031 by striking "2026" and inserting "2031" in Section 7 of Public Law 117-79.
items.detail: Section 7 of the 2021 Act authorized $100M for each of fiscal years 2022 through 2026 to carry out the whole Act. This bill's Section 2(a) resets the terminal fiscal year to 2031, continuing the same $100M-per-year authorization ceiling for five more fiscal years without raising the annual amount.

items.main: Extends the sunset on the ALS investigational-drug grants program from September 30, 2026 to September 30, 2031 by amending Section 2(f) of the 2021 Act (21 U.S.C. 360ee note).
items.detail: Under the 2021 Act, HHS may not award new grants under the Section 2 expanded-access research program on or after September 30, 2026. This bill's Section 2(b) strikes "2026" and inserts "2031" in that sunset clause, letting the Secretary continue awarding grants for another five fiscal years.

items.main: Requires HHS to request and assess enrollment, safety, and any available efficacy data on the investigational drug when reviewing grant-renewal applications under the ALS research program.
items.detail: The 2021 Act's Section 2 authorizes grants to participating entities using data from expanded access to investigational drugs for ALS. This bill adds a new paragraph (4) to Section 2(b) directing that, on renewals, the Secretary shall request from the manufacturer or sponsor — and assess — enrollment, safety, and any available efficacy data relating to the drug's use in preventing, diagnosing, mitigating, treating, or curing ALS.

items.main: Requires grantees to promptly report new and serious adverse events and unexpected safety information from their phase 3 trial to the grant-making institution, on top of existing FDA safety-reporting rules.
items.detail: This adds paragraph (4) to Section 2(c) of the 2021 Act. Grantees must report to the grant-making institution in addition to complying with the safety reporting requirements under section 312.32 of title 21, Code of Federal Regulations (or any successor regulations).

items.main: Expands the definition of "phase 3" for participating clinical trials to include phase 2/3 combined trials that begin enrollment within a Secretary-determined timeframe.
items.detail: Under the 2021 Act, participating clinical trials had to be phase 3 trials conducted pursuant to an investigational new drug exemption under section 505(i) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act. This bill's Section 3(c) adds paragraph (4) to Section 2(e) so that combined phase 2/3 trials also qualify as "phase 3" if they begin enrollment within a timeframe the Secretary sets in the grant's terms and conditions.

sections.label: Section 4 — FDA Rare Neurodegenerative Disease Action Plan

items.main: Renames the section heading and requires FDA to publish a new rare-neurodegenerative-disease action plan on the FDA website within 18 months of enactment, covering the following 5-year period.
items.detail: Section 4 of the 2021 Act (21 U.S.C. 360aa note) already directed the FDA Commissioner to publish a rare-neurodegenerative-disease action plan within 6 months of that Act's December 2021 enactment. This bill renames the section heading from "als and other rare neurodegenerative disease action plan" to "fda rare neurodegenerative disease action plan" and adds subsection (c)(1), requiring a new plan within 18 months of enactment of this Reauthorization Act that describes actions FDA intends to take over the 5-year period following publication with respect to program enhancements, policy development, regulatory science initiatives, and other initiatives described in subsection (a).

items.main: Requires FDA to publish a follow-up report on the FDA website within 5 years of enactment describing actions taken under the new action plan and the extent to which it meets the requirements.
items.detail: Subsection (c)(2) sets a 5-year post-enactment deadline for the Commissioner of Food and Drugs to publish a report describing what FDA actually did under the action plan required by paragraph (1) and the extent to which that plan meets the paragraph (1) requirements. The bill sets no penalty or consequence if the plan or report is late or omits required elements.

underreported.summary: The bill expands "phase 3" for grant-eligibility purposes to include phase 2/3 combined trials, and lets the HHS Secretary set the enrollment-start timeframe through the grant's terms and conditions rather than in statute.
underreported.why_unreported: The section is captioned as "Clarifying Participating Clinical Trial Definition," but the operative effect is to broaden which drug-development stages qualify for the ALS grants program and to leave the enrollment-window boundary to Secretary discretion rather than a statutory number.

underreported.summary: The bill renames the underlying Section 4 heading from "ALS and other rare neurodegenerative disease action plan" to "FDA rare neurodegenerative disease action plan," dropping the explicit ALS reference from the section title.
underreported.why_unreported: The reauthorization is framed around ALS, but the retitled Section 4 shifts the framing of the FDA action plan from an ALS-anchored plan to a general rare-neurodegenerative-disease plan without changing the substantive scope.

gaps: The bill extends the underlying Act's $100M-per-year authorization through fiscal year 2031 but does not itself appropriate any money — the actual dollars still depend on annual appropriations.

The bill retitles Section 4 as an "FDA rare neurodegenerative disease action plan" but does not extend or reauthorize the Section 5 FDA Rare Neurodegenerative Disease Grant Program (21 U.S.C. 360ee-1) separately.

The bill requires grantees to promptly report serious adverse events to the grant-making institution but does not define "promptly," specify a maximum reporting window, or provide penalties for non-reporting beyond the existing 21 C.F.R. § 312.32 obligations.

The bill requires an FDA action plan and 5-year report on rare neurodegenerative diseases but does not require any consultation with patient organizations, ALS advocacy groups, or the public-private partnership established in Section 3 of the 2021 Act.

The reauthorization does not address the HHS Public-Private Partnership for Rare Neurodegenerative Diseases established in Section 3 of the 2021 Act — the Partnership continues under the extended Section 7 authorization but this bill adds no new requirements or metrics for it.

added: New requirement that HHS request and assess enrollment, safety, and any available efficacy data when reviewing renewals of ALS investigational-drug research grants
New requirement that grantees promptly report new and serious adverse events and unexpected safety information to the grant-making institution
New FDA action-plan publication requirement (18 months after enactment) covering a 5-year period, and a follow-up report requirement (5 years after enactment)
modified: Section 7 of the 2021 Act — authorization of appropriations terminal fiscal year 2026 → 2031
Section 2(f) of the 2021 Act — grants sunset date September 30, 2026 → September 30, 2031
Section 2(e) of the 2021 Act — "phase 3" definition expanded to include phase 2/3 combined trials that begin enrollment within a Secretary-determined timeframe
Section 4 heading of the 2021 Act — renamed from "ALS and other rare neurodegenerative disease action plan" to "FDA rare neurodegenerative disease action plan"

bills.title: Billion Dollar Boondoggle Act
bills.official_title: To require an annual report of taxpayer-funded projects that are over budget and behind schedule.
bills.likelihoodReason: Introduced by Rep. Miller-Meeks (R-IA-1) with 3 cosponsors and cleared the House on July 22, 2026 before being received in the Senate. The bill's operative content is an OMB reporting requirement on cost-overrun and schedule-slip projects, with no new spending, penalties, or rights created — the kind of transparency mandate that historically draws limited floor opposition in either chamber. The main friction points are executive-branch resistance to new reporting workload (particularly on major defense acquisition programs, which are within scope) and Senate calendar time rather than substantive opposition.
bills.summary: This bill requires the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) to publish an annual report identifying federal projects that are more than five years behind schedule or at least $1B over their original cost estimate. Federal agencies must submit a defined set of information on each qualifying project — descriptions, contractors, cost histories, and any bonuses paid — so OMB can compile it for Congress and post it publicly.
bills.brief: Creates an annual public OMB report listing federal projects that are five-plus years late or over $1B above original cost estimate, with detailed data on each.

top_lines.headline: What Triggers a Report
subs: Project is more than 5 years behind its original expected completion date, or
Project has spent at least $1B more than its original cost estimate
Applies to executive agencies and independent regulatory agencies

top_lines.headline: Required Project Information
subs: Purpose, locations, contract or award number, and start year of each project
Every primary contractor, subcontractor, grant recipient, and subgrantee
Original vs. current completion date and CPI-adjusted cost estimate
Amount and rationale for every award, incentive fee, or bonus paid

top_lines.headline: OMB Timing & Delivery
subs: OMB must issue agency-reporting guidance within 1 year of enactment
Annual report submitted to Congress and posted on the OMB website
Report is unclassified but may include a classified annex

items.main: Defines the projects covered as those funded by executive or independent regulatory agencies that are either more than 5 years behind schedule or at least $1B over their original cost estimate.
items.detail: Section 2(a) draws "covered agency" from the executive agency definition in 5 U.S.C. 105 plus the independent regulatory agency definition in 44 U.S.C. 3502. "Project" includes major acquisitions, major defense acquisition programs (using the 10 U.S.C. 4201 definition), procurements, construction projects, and remediation or clean-up efforts, but excludes direct spending as defined in 2 U.S.C. 900(c) of the Balanced Budget and Emergency Deficit Control Act of 1985.

items.main: Requires OMB to issue guidance within 1 year of enactment directing covered agencies to annually submit a detailed information package on each covered project.
items.detail: For each covered project, agencies must supply the purpose, every location where it is carried out, the contract or award number where applicable, the year it was initiated, the federal share of total cost, and every primary contractor, subcontractor, grant recipient, and subgrantee. Agencies must also submit any changes to the original scope, original and current completion dates, original and current cost estimates adjusted using the Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers, an explanation for delays or cost increases (including any impact of insufficient or delayed appropriations), and the amount of and rationale for any award, incentive fee, or bonus.

items.main: Directs OMB to submit an annual report to Congress compiling the agency submissions and to post the report on the OMB website.
items.detail: The report must be submitted in unclassified form but may include a classified annex, allowing sensitive defense or intelligence project details to be withheld from public view while still reaching Congress. The bill sets no explicit remedies, penalties, or funding cutoffs for projects that appear on the list — the mechanism is disclosure only.

underreported.summary: The definition of "project" explicitly includes major defense acquisition programs (using the 10 U.S.C. 4201 definition), meaning cost-overrun defense procurements would appear on the same public list as civilian projects.
underreported.why_unreported: The bill's short title frames it as a general government-waste measure, but the operative definition pulls in the Pentagon's largest acquisition programs, which are the projects most prone to multi-year delays and multi-billion-dollar cost growth.

underreported.summary: Direct-spending programs are excluded from the covered-project definition by cross-reference to 2 U.S.C. 900(c).
underreported.why_unreported: The "boondoggle" framing suggests all wasteful federal spending, but mandatory-spending programs — the largest share of the federal budget — are structurally outside the report's scope.

gaps: The bill requires reporting on cost-overrun and schedule-slip projects but does not create any remedy, penalty, corrective action, or funding trigger tied to a project appearing on the list.
The bill lists what OMB must publish but does not specify a data format, machine-readability requirement, or update cadence beyond "annual," leaving the utility of the disclosure to OMB discretion.

The bill requires agencies to disclose every primary contractor and subcontractor on covered projects but does not address whether contractors may claim confidential-business-information exemptions on the underlying data.

The bill excludes direct spending from the covered-project definition but does not address whether tax expenditures, credit programs, or federally guaranteed loans should be tracked separately when they exhibit similar cost or schedule slippage.
The bill applies to independent regulatory agencies as defined in 44 U.S.C. 3502 but does not address enforcement if such an agency declines to submit the required information to OMB.

added: New annual OMB report requirement covering federal projects more than 5 years behind schedule or at least $1B over original cost estimate
New agency obligation to compile and submit CPI-adjusted cost histories, contractor lists, and bonus rationales for each covered project

bills.title: Stop Insider Trading Act
bills.official_title: To amend chapter 131 of title 5 to require certain restrictions on stocks for Members of Congress and their spouses and dependents, and for other purposes.
bills.likelihoodReason: Introduced by Rep. Steil (R-WI-1) with 93 cosponsors and cleared the House on July 22, 2026 before being received in the Senate. The stock-trading restriction (Section 2) is the kind of proposal that has drawn broad bipartisan support in prior Congresses, but the House-passed version also contains a Section 3 photo-identification requirement for federal elections that is not part of the bill's short title or CRS summary — a rider likely to draw uniform Democratic opposition in the Senate and effectively block the 60-vote cloture threshold. The two-track structure means the insider-trading provisions are unlikely to advance unless the voter-ID section is stripped in Senate negotiation.
bills.summary: This bill has two operative sections. Section 2 bars Members of Congress and their spouses and dependent children from purchasing individual stocks, requires 7-to-14-day advance public notice before selling, and imposes a fee (greater of $2,000 or ten percent of transaction value, plus any net gain) for violations. Section 3 amends the Help America Vote Act to require in-person federal-election voters to present a state, federal, or Tribal photo identification, and mail voters to submit either a photo-ID copy, their last four Social Security digits with an affidavit, or a notarization.
bills.brief: Bans stock purchases and requires advance sale notices for Members of Congress and their spouses/dependents, and separately requires photo ID for all federal-election voting.

top_lines.headline: Congressional Stock-Trading Ban
subs: Members of Congress, their spouses, and their dependent children may not purchase covered investments
Sales require public notice 7 to 14 calendar days before the sale, filed with the Clerk or Secretary and posted online
Covers securities of publicly traded companies and derivative equivalents like options and warrants

top_lines.headline: Exemptions from the Trading Ban
subs: Excepted investment funds (as described in section 13104(f)(8)) and comparable US-, state-, or territory-concentrated funds
Interests in small business concerns
Trusts where no covered individual has authority over the trustee, and the trustee is not a Member's spouse, child, parent, or sibling
Spouse or dependent trades made as part of a primary occupation or employer compensation, and automatic dividend reinvestments

top_lines.headline: Enforcement
subs: Fee equal to the greater of $2,000 or ten percent of the transaction value, plus any net gain realized
Fee cannot be paid from the Members' Representational Allowance, Senators' Official Personnel and Office Expense Account, or campaign contributions
Ethics office may refer former Members to DOJ if they resign or retire before paying

top_lines.headline: Federal Photo-ID Voting Requirement
subs: In-person federal-election voters must present a valid physical photo identification
Mail voters must submit a photo-ID copy, last four SSN digits with an inability affidavit, or notarization
Provisional ballot available if ID missing; ID or religious-photography-objection affidavit must be produced within 3 days

top_lines.headline: Accepted ID Types and State Duties
subs: State driver's license or ID card (with photo and expiration), U.S. passport, DoD or VA photo ID card, or Tribal-government ID with photo and expiration
States must provide free access to a digital imaging device (printer, copier, scanner) at courts, libraries, and police stations
States must notify voters of the ID requirement at registration and during online registration

items.main: Adds new Subchapter IV to chapter 131 of title 5, U.S. Code, prohibiting Members of Congress and their spouses and dependent children from purchasing individual securities of publicly traded companies or derivative equivalents.
items.detail: New section 13152(a) bars any "covered individual" from purchasing a covered investment, and section 13151 defines covered individuals as Members of Congress plus spouses and dependent children, and covered investments as publicly traded company securities or comparable synthetic interests (options, warrants, other derivatives). The prohibition takes effect 180 days after enactment.

items.main: Requires public advance notice 7 to 14 calendar days before any sale of a covered investment, filed with the Clerk of the House or Secretary of the Senate and posted online.
items.detail: New section 13152(b) requires each Member to file a notice of intent to sell — including projected sale date, description, and number of shares — for their own or a covered spouse or dependent's sale, no less than 7 and no more than 14 calendar days before the sale. The Clerk or Secretary must publish the notice and any withdrawal on a public website, and the notice must be withdrawn if the sale is called off.

items.main: Sets enforcement through a fee equal to the greater of $2,000 or ten percent of the transaction value, plus any net gain realized during the coverage period, and imposes divestiture for illegal purchases.
items.detail: New section 13153 directs the supervising ethics office to impose the fee on the Member who caused the violation (or whose spouse or child did) and to require the sale of any covered investment purchased in violation of section 13152(a). Members may not pay the fee from the Members' Representational Allowance, Senators' Official Personnel and Office Expense Account, campaign contributions (as defined in section 301(8) of the Federal Election Campaign Act of 1971), or other Federal-office donations. Fees are deposited to the Treasury general fund as miscellaneous receipts. The ethics office may refer a former Member who resigns or retires before paying to the Department of Justice, with section 13106 applied the same as for a direct violation.

sections.label: Section 3 — Photo Identification Requirements for Federal Elections

items.main: Adds a new section 303A to the Help America Vote Act of 2002 (52 U.S.C. 21081 et seq.) requiring in-person voters in federal elections to present a valid physical photo identification.
items.detail: State or local election officials may not provide an in-person federal-election ballot without a valid physical photo ID. A voter without ID may cast a provisional ballot but the eligibility determination under HAVA section 302(a)(4) may not be made unless, within 3 days, the voter presents the required ID or an affidavit — developed and made available by the State — attesting to a religious objection to being photographed.

items.main: Requires mail and other non-in-person voters to submit a photo-ID copy, the last four digits of their Social Security number plus an inability affidavit, or a notarization by a notary public.
items.detail: New section 303A(a)(2) blocks acceptance of non-in-person ballots unless the voter submits (i) a copy of a valid photo identification, (ii) the last four SSN digits and a state-provided affidavit attesting to inability to obtain a copy after reasonable efforts, or (iii) a notary-attested statement that the voter personally marked the ballot. Exempted are absent uniformed services voters as defined in section 107(1) of the Uniformed and Overseas Citizens Absentee Voting Act (52 U.S.C. 20310(1)) and individuals voting under section 3(b)(2)(B)(ii) of the Voting Accessibility for the Elderly and Handicapped Act.

items.main: Defines the accepted forms of valid photo identification and imposes new state duties to publicize the requirement and to provide free public access to copying equipment.
items.detail: Accepted IDs are: a State-issued driver's license or motor-vehicle-authority ID card (each with photo and expiration date), a valid U.S. passport, a DoD or VA photo ID card, or a photo ID document with expiration date issued by a Tribal government. States must ensure, to the extent practicable, free public access to a digital imaging device (printer, copier, image scanner, or multifunction machine) at state and local government buildings including courts, libraries, and police stations, for making photo-ID copies. States must notify individuals of the photo-ID requirement at the time of voter registration, including before completion of online registration. Section 3 takes effect 90 days after enactment.

underreported.summary: The bill inserts a new HAVA section 303A imposing a federal photo-ID requirement on all in-person voting and a photo-ID or SSN-plus-affidavit requirement on all non-in-person voting in federal elections.
underreported.why_unreported: The bill's short title is the "Stop Insider Trading Act" and the CRS summary describes only the stock-trading restrictions on Members of Congress. The photo-ID rule is a stand-alone federal election-administration mandate on all states, mechanically unrelated to the insider-trading subject in the title.

underreported.summary: Section 401 of HAVA (52 U.S.C. 21111), which sets the Department of Justice enforcement scope for HAVA voting requirements, is amended so its scope reads "subtitle A of title III" instead of the current "sections 301, 302, 303, and 304."
underreported.why_unreported: The section is labeled "Conforming Amendment Relating to Enforcement," but the change replaces four enumerated sections with a broader reference to the entire subtitle, which expands the range of HAVA provisions covered by the DOJ enforcement authority beyond the four sections currently named.

underreported.summary: The stock-purchase ban applies to a Member's spouse and dependent children as well as the Member.
underreported.why_unreported: The public-facing framing focuses on Members' own trading; the operative rule reaches household-member portfolios, subject to the occupational and dividend-reinvestment exceptions in section 13152(c).

underreported.summary: The enforcement fee includes not just $2,000 or ten percent but also any net gain realized on the covered investment from the date the individual became a covered individual through disposition.
underreported.why_unreported: The headline penalty is "$2,000 or ten percent," but the second, uncapped component can vastly exceed the flat or percentage fee for a long-held position that appreciated during a covered individual's tenure.

gaps: The bill bans covered individuals from purchasing new covered investments but does not require Members already holding covered investments on the effective date to divest, nor set any deadline for disposing of pre-existing holdings.

The bill's insider-trading restrictions apply only to Members of Congress, spouses, and dependent children — the bill does not address covered financial holdings of Executive Branch officials, federal judges, or Congressional staff.

Section 3 requires a valid photo identification for federal-election voting but does not appropriate any funds to help states issue free voter-eligible ID cards or to operate the required copying devices at courts, libraries, and police stations.

Section 3 provides a religious-photography-objection affidavit path but no equivalent affidavit path for voters who lack photo identification for non-religious reasons (e.g. lost, stolen, expired, or unaffordable ID) at in-person voting.

The bill's enforcement mechanism for the insider-trading section is a fee plus divestiture — the bill does not create a criminal penalty for a Member who trades on non-public information, leaving that conduct to existing securities law.

added: New Subchapter IV of chapter 131 of title 5, U.S. Code (new sections 13151, 13152, 13153) — stock-trading restrictions on Members of Congress and covered household members
New section 303A of the Help America Vote Act — federal-election photo identification requirement for in-person and non-in-person voting
modified: Table of contents for chapter 131 of title 5, U.S. Code — new Subchapter IV entries added
HAVA section 311(b) (52 U.S.C. 21101(b)) — new paragraph (4) directing Election Assistance Commission voluntary guidance on section 303A within 90 days of enactment
HAVA section 401 (52 U.S.C. 21111) — enforcement scope changed from "sections 301, 302, 303, and 304" to "subtitle A of title III"

bills.title: National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2027
bills.official_title: To authorize appropriations for fiscal year 2027 for military activities of the Department of Defense, for military construction, and for defense activities of the Department of Energy, to prescribe military personnel strengths for such fiscal year, and for other purposes.
bills.likelihoodReason: The annual NDAA has been enacted into law every fiscal year for more than six consecutive decades. This House-passed version was introduced by House Armed Services Chairman Rogers (R-AL-3) with Ranking Member Smith (D-WA-9) as an original cosponsor, and cleared the House on July 22, 2026. Remaining variables are Senate committee markup, floor amendments in either chamber, and the conference-committee outcome on the more contested provisions — Section 1655 space-based interceptors, Section 1246 Taiwan Security Cooperation Initiative funding, Sections 1221-1223 Israel cooperation extensions, Section 1237 NATO burden-sharing reports, and Section 1247 Korean Peninsula posture funding limits. None of those disputes have historically been large enough to prevent an NDAA from being enacted before the fiscal year ends.
bills.summary: This is the annual defense authorization bill for fiscal year 2027, organized into four divisions covering the Department of Defense, military construction, Department of Energy defense-related programs, and the funding tables that give effect to the authorizations. Section 401 sets active-duty end strengths of 469,000 Army; 356,600 Navy; 173,700 Marine Corps; 330,400 Air Force; and 13,200 Space Force. Division B authorizes named military construction projects by service branch — Army, Navy, Air Force, Defense Agencies, and NATO Security Investment Program — plus separate Guard and Reserve construction authorizations. On the personnel side, Section 632 raises the death gratuity payable to survivors from $100,000 to $165,000 with annual Consumer Price Index adjustment beginning January 1, 2027, and Section 706 requires TRICARE to cover up to a 365-day supply of contraception on the uniform formulary. Foreign-policy items include a Section 1246 authorization of up to $1.00B for the Taiwan Security Cooperation Initiative, Section 1221 extension of the Israel war reserve stockpile authority through January 1, 2029, and Section 1237 quarterly NATO burden-sharing reports evaluating allied progress toward the 5 percent defense investment commitment agreed at the 2025 Hague Summit. Division C Section 3501 authorizes $873.5M for the U.S. Merchant Marine Academy and separately funds the Maritime Security Program ($400.5M), Tanker Security Fleet ($167.6M), Cable Security Fleet ($30M), port infrastructure ($550M), small shipyards ($105M), and other Maritime Administration programs.
bills.brief: The FY2027 defense authorization bill — sets DoD/DOE-defense/military construction spending ceilings, personnel end strengths, and dozens of policy provisions from Taiwan and Israel cooperation to a new AI Model Rapid Deployment Framework and a $1.97B-plus military construction program.

top_lines.headline: Authorizes FY2027 DoD Spending Levels and Sets Force Sizes
subs: Sections 101, 201, 301, and 421 authorize appropriations for procurement, research/development/test/evaluation, operation and maintenance, and military personnel — with the specific dollar amounts set out in the Division D funding tables (Sections 4101, 4201, 4301, 4401)
Section 401 sets active-duty end strengths as of September 30, 2027: Army 469,000; Navy 356,600; Marine Corps 173,700; Air Force 330,400; Space Force 13,200

Section 411 sets Selected Reserve strengths: Army National Guard 331,300; Army Reserve 172,000; Navy Reserve 56,500; Marine Corps Reserve 34,700; Air National Guard 107,400; Air Force Reserve 67,400; Coast Guard Reserve 8,500
Section 1001 provides $6.00B in general transfer authority letting the Secretary of Defense move funds between accounts within the authorization

top_lines.headline: Military Construction Across the Services
subs: Section 2101 authorizes $1.97B for Army construction and land acquisition (10 items)
Section 2201 authorizes $19.25B for Navy construction and land acquisition (18 items)
Section 2301 authorizes $9.94B for Air Force construction and land acquisition (30 items)
Section 2401 authorizes $5.24B for Defense Agencies construction and land acquisition (21 items), plus Section 2402 authorizes $694.3M for the Energy Resilience and Conservation Investment Program
Section 2501 authorizes $604.3M for NATO Security Investment Program construction projects

top_lines.headline: Servicemember Pay, Benefits, and Family Provisions
subs: Section 632 raises the death gratuity payable to survivors of a servicemember killed on active duty from $100,000 to $165,000, applicable to deaths on or after enactment, and adds a Consumer Price Index cost-of-living adjustment beginning January 1, 2027

Section 706 requires TRICARE to cover a supply of up to 365 days of a contraceptive on the uniform formulary — including in a single fill or refill — for members on active duty and their dependents, starting no later than 180 days after enactment

Section 612 makes permanent the authority under 37 USC 403 for the Secretary concerned to make an equitable Basic Allowance for Housing determination for a member without dependents assigned to sea duty
Section 615 authorizes the Department to pay the cost of shipping breast milk for a servicemember mother performing duty away from her nursing child
Section 601 extends most expiring bonus, incentive-pay, and special-pay authorities from December 31, 2026 to December 31, 2027

top_lines.headline: Foreign-Policy Provisions: Israel, Taiwan, NATO, China, Korea
subs: Section 1246 authorizes up to $1.00B for the Taiwan Security Cooperation Initiative for fiscal year 2027

Section 1221 extends the U.S. war reserve stockpile authority for Israel from January 1, 2027 to January 1, 2029; Section 1222 renames the U.S.-Israel anti-tunnel cooperation program "subterranean" and extends it through 2029; Section 1223 extends U.S.-Israel counter-unmanned-systems cooperation through 2029

Section 1237 requires the U.S. European Command Commander to submit 90-day reports through January 1, 2028 on allied progress toward the 5 percent defense-investment commitment agreed at the 2025 Hague NATO Summit, and on force posture and readiness on NATO's eastern flank

Section 1247 extends existing restrictions on obligating or expending U.S. funds for changes to U.S. military posture on the Korean Peninsula to cover fiscal year 2027 amounts as well as fiscal year 2026
Section 1722 requires a classified report on Russian and Chinese intelligence penetration in Georgia, plus a 5-year State Department strategy for bilateral relations with Georgia

top_lines.headline: Emerging Technology and Missile-Defense Provisions
subs: Section 1523 directs the Chief Digital and Artificial Intelligence Officer to establish an AI Model Rapid Deployment Framework, with the objective of deploying artificial intelligence systems on Department enterprise AI platforms within 30 days after public availability

Section 1655 requires the Director of Cost Assessment and Program Evaluation to conduct an independent life-cycle cost estimate of the space-based interceptor program, and bars a full-rate production contract until the Secretary certifies at least one successful operationally relevant flight test
Section 1656 directs the Missile Defense Agency to develop and demonstrate a low-cost exo-atmospheric interceptor complementary to existing ballistic-missile-defense interceptors

Section 3111 rewrites 10 USC 6128(a) to require the Department of Energy to ensure the nuclear security enterprise has the capability to reliably produce no fewer than 180 war reserve plutonium pits annually by not later than 2050

Section 1811 requires annual reports through 2032 on supply-chain dependencies for biotechnology equipment and services, including a classified annex identifying any biotechnology company of concern being considered for OMB designation

items.main: Titles I through XVIII cover procurement, research-and-development, operation and maintenance, military personnel, personnel policy, compensation, health care, acquisition policy, DoD organization, general provisions, civilian personnel, foreign nations, other authorizations, cyberspace, space and strategic programs, other defense matters, and revitalization of the defense industrial base.
items.detail: The dollar amounts for procurement, RDT&E, O&M, military personnel, and other authorizations are set out in the Division D funding tables under Sections 4101, 4201, 4301, 4401, and 4501, incorporated by reference under Section 4001. Section 1001 authorizes the Secretary of Defense to transfer up to $6.00B between accounts within the authorization, subject to notification requirements.

items.main: Includes numerous authorities on specific weapon systems: Section 123 authorizes a multiyear procurement contract for up to 15 Arleigh Burke Flight III destroyers; Section 124 authorizes multiyear procurement for John Lewis class oilers; Section 127 authorizes multiyear procurement for E-2D Advanced Hawkeye aircraft; Section 128 authorizes incremental funding for ship-to-shore connector construction.
items.detail: Section 123(e) caps modifications to the destroyer multiyear contract at 10 percent above the original target price. Section 123(d) requires that if fewer than 15 destroyers are procured through the base contracts, one or more contracts must include a prepriced option so the base plus option quantity reaches 15. Section 122 gives the Navy incremental funding authority for long-lead components on Virginia class submarines.

items.main: Section 142 extends the existing statutory prohibition on retiring F-22 aircraft; Sections 143, 145, 146, and 147 impose or extend limitations on retirement or availability of E-3 AWACS, C-130, C-37, and MQ-9 Reaper aircraft.
items.detail: Section 144 requires the Air Force to evaluate the potential transfer of certain A-10 aircraft. Section 141 sets minimum inventory requirements for certain fighter aircraft. These provisions constrain the services' ability to divest older platforms during FY2027.

items.main: Authorizes named construction and land-acquisition projects at specific installations by service branch — $1.97B Army (Section 2101), $19.25B Navy (Section 2201), $9.94B Air Force (Section 2301), $5.24B Defense Agencies (Section 2401), $604.3M NATO Security Investment Program (Section 2501), plus $694.3M for the Energy Resilience and Conservation Investment Program (Section 2402).
items.detail: Guard and Reserve construction is authorized separately under Sections 2601-2605: Army National Guard $225.5M, Army Reserve $178.0M, Navy Reserve and Marine Corps Reserve $47.0M, Air National Guard $531.0M, Air Force Reserve $19.5M. Sections 2511 and 2512 authorize $416.5M in Republic of Korea funded projects and $134.0M in Republic of Poland funded projects.

items.main: Extends the authority to carry out named military construction projects authorized in prior fiscal years but not yet completed — Section 2108 extends fiscal-year projects with a $656.4M summed value across 11 items; Section 2205 extends Navy projects with a $2.43B summed value across 14 items; Section 2307 extends Air Force projects with a $1.31B summed value across 19 items; Section 2405 extends Defense Agencies projects with a $555.4M summed value across 12 items.
items.detail: Section 2607 and Section 2608 similarly extend Guard and Reserve project authorities with summed values of $323.7M and $349.9M respectively. Section 2802 adds Tribal governments to the list of entities eligible for defense community infrastructure program grants. Section 2804 raises unspecified minor military construction dollar thresholds.

sections.label: Division C — DOE Defense Programs and Maritime (Titles XXXI–XXXVI)

items.main: Section 3101 authorizes the Department of Energy's National Nuclear Security Administration activities for fiscal year 2027 per the funding table in Section 4701, and specifically authorizes a new $88.7M Plutonium Engineering Support Building at Los Alamos National Laboratory.
items.detail: Section 3102 authorizes defense environmental cleanup, Section 3103 authorizes other defense activities, and Section 3104 authorizes nuclear energy — all per the Section 4701 funding table. Section 3111 rewrites 10 USC 6128(a) to set the plutonium pit production capability requirement at 180 pits annually by not later than 2050, and shifts the pit-production report from annual to "each odd numbered year." Section 3112 changes the federal cost share for accelerating replacement of cesium blood irradiation sources from 50 percent to 100 percent of the per-device cost.

items.main: Section 3501 authorizes $873.5M for the U.S. Merchant Marine Academy in fiscal year 2027 — of which $129.5M is for Academy operations, $120M is for facilities and infrastructure under the Campus Modernization Plan, and $624M is for capital improvement projects.
items.detail: Section 3501 also authorizes $53.4M for State maritime academies (including $9.4M for the Student Incentive Payment Program), $75M for the National Security Multi-Mission Vessel program, $105.76M for Maritime Administration operations, $6M for disposal of obsolete vessels, $400.5M for the Maritime Security Program, $30M for the Cable Security Fleet, $167.6M for the Tanker Security Fleet, $33.7M for the Federal Ship Financing Program (Title XI loan guarantees), $105M for the Small Shipyards Program, $550M for the Port Infrastructure Development Program, and $300M in maritime incentive payments to designated centers of excellence. Section 3531 requires the President to submit implementation proposals for the February 2026 White House Maritime Action Plan within 90 days of enactment.

underreported.summary: Section 3111 sets a 2050 target date for the Department of Energy's plutonium-pit production capability of 180 pits per year — a long-horizon commitment on a key nuclear-weapons enterprise metric that receives little coverage compared with weapon-system authorizations.
underreported.why_unreported: Plutonium pit production capacity is a technical nuclear-enterprise milestone rather than a headline weapon system, and the bill also downshifts the associated report from annual to every other year, further reducing the frequency at which the milestone gets public attention.

underreported.summary: Section 1655 imposes hard gates on the space-based interceptor program — no full-rate production contract until the Director of Cost Assessment and Program Evaluation completes an independent life-cycle cost estimate, and no full-rate production decision until at least one successful operationally relevant flight test has occurred.
underreported.why_unreported: The public debate over space-based interceptors focuses on whether to pursue them at all, so procedural cost-and-test gates that constrain how quickly the Missile Defense Agency can move the program to production tend to be overlooked.

underreported.summary: Section 3501 authorizes a broad slate of Maritime Administration programs — Merchant Marine Academy, State maritime academies, Maritime Security Program, Tanker Security Fleet, Cable Security Fleet, port infrastructure, small shipyards, and centers of excellence — inside a defense authorization bill rather than a transportation or maritime bill.
underreported.why_unreported: The Maritime Administration is a Department of Transportation agency, not a DoD component, so its authorization being packaged in the NDAA as Division C, Title XXXV places substantial DOT program funding outside the visibility of most transportation-policy coverage.

new: Section 1523 creates a new Artificial Intelligence Model Rapid Deployment Framework at the Chief Digital and Artificial Intelligence Officer, targeting a 30-day deployment window for AI systems onto Department enterprise AI platforms after public availability.

Section 1811 establishes annual reports through 2032 identifying supply-chain dependencies for biotechnology equipment and services obtained by the Department of Defense, with a classified annex identifying covered foreign entities being considered for biotechnology-company-of-concern designation.

Section 3113 creates new Other Transaction Authority for the National Nuclear Security Administration Administrator, adapting the DoD Section 4021/4022 acquisition authorities for the nuclear security enterprise.
Section 3531 requires the President to submit implementation proposals for the February 2026 White House Maritime Action Plan within 90 days of enactment.
modified: Section 632 raises the death gratuity from $100,000 to $165,000 and adds a permanent Consumer Price Index annual adjustment beginning January 1, 2027.

Section 706 expands the TRICARE contraceptive benefit to include a single-fill or refill supply of up to 365 days at military pharmacies, retail network pharmacies, and the national mail-order pharmacy.
Section 1246 modifies the Taiwan Security Cooperation Initiative to authorize up to $1.00B of the fiscal-year-2027 DoD authorization for the initiative's purposes.
Section 1221 extends the Israel war reserve stockpile authority under Section 12001(d) of the 2005 DoD Appropriations Act from January 1, 2027 to January 1, 2029.

Section 3111 rewrites 10 USC 6128(a) to set the plutonium-pit production-capability requirement at 180 pits annually by not later than 2050, and shifts the associated congressional report from annual to every other year.
Section 3112 raises the federal cost share for replacing cesium blood irradiation sources from 50 percent to 100 percent of the per-device cost.

gaps: The bill does not itself set the FY2027 basic-pay-raise percentage — that adjustment continues to be governed by the annual Employment Cost Index formula under 37 USC 1009 absent a specific NDAA override.
The bill authorizes appropriations but does not itself appropriate money — actual funding flows through a separate Defense Appropriations Act that must clear both chambers.

The bill contains no free-standing policy on Ukraine security assistance, and no provisions specifically addressing operations at the southern border, both of which have been contested topics in prior NDAAs.
